title: Empiric medicines that cover the major causes of severe acute viral disease

concept.text: The proposed innovation is one practically deliverable antiviral regimen, or a very small formulary, that clinicians could start before identifying the virus in a patient with severe acute disease. Its intended scope is the major families of acute human RNA viruses, especially those without effective treatments. The advance would be clinically demonstrated coverage across these causes of disease, with a usable approach to choosing treatment while diagnostic results are pending. The supplied evidence supports this therapeutic goal but does not establish that it has been achieved.

A portfolio could combine drugs active against related viruses within a genus, drugs spanning a viral family, and agents with activity across multiple families. Direct-acting drugs would inhibit viral machinery; host-directed drugs would interfere with cellular processes that several viruses depend on. These strategies could contribute complementary coverage. Breadth in laboratory assays would be an initial finding, while the proposed capability requires safe, effective treatment in people.

Scope synthesis: a single safe medicine effective against every RNA and DNA virus would exceed the intended breadth, but the concept does not require that outcome. Nor does it require preventing infection, producing lasting immunity, or eliminating latent viral genomes. Those are separate capabilities. Treatment begun before identification also differs from treatment of an entirely novel virus: the former can be demonstrated with known infections whose diagnostic results arrive later.

significance.text: Many life-threatening viral infections still lack effective therapeutics, and approved antiviral coverage is generally narrow. A safe formulary with demonstrated efficacy across major causes of severe acute RNA-virus disease would allow treatment to begin during the interval before accurate pathogen identification. Conditional on achieving that breadth and clinical benefit, this would substantially expand treatment options in both ordinary severe-disease care and outbreak response.

Broad antiviral activity could also improve preparedness for newly emerging pathogens and create treatment options for uncommon infections that attract little disease-specific drug development. These benefits would depend on whether the actual causative virus falls within the regimen's demonstrated or subsequently confirmed coverage. Activity against known relatives would provide a rationale for investigation, rather than a guarantee of benefit against an unseen virus.

Interpretive analogy: the useful comparison with empiric antibiotics is the ability to treat a dangerous syndrome before identifying its precise microbial cause. It does not establish that antiviral coverage, safety, or clinical performance would resemble antibacterial treatment. The proposed formulary would have defined coverage gaps and patient-specific limits. The supplied evidence establishes neither the existence nor the frequency of a universal antiviral target, and it does not support a prediction that one molecule will eventually cover all viruses.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is reliable clinical breadth: translating activity against multiple viruses into improved outcomes for patients with severe acute infections across a specified range of viral families. Viral proteins commonly differ substantially in sequence and structure, which limits the reach of many direct-acting drugs. This is a general constraint rather than an absolute rule. Conserved catalytic structures in viral polymerases offer opportunities for broader inhibition, but conservation alone does not establish a clinically effective spectrum.

Host-directed treatment offers another route because unrelated viruses can depend on shared cellular factors. The engineering challenge is to disrupt those dependencies sufficiently to suppress infection while preserving essential host functions. A short treatment course still requires evidence of an acceptable therapeutic margin. Toxicity and the limited translation of protection in preclinical models into human clinical benefit remain major barriers.

Practical delivery is part of the breakthrough. The medicines must reach useful exposures through oral administration or another route workable in the intended care setting, remain tolerable at effective doses, and retain benefit over the treatment course. Resistance must also be assessed rather than assumed to be rare because a drug targets a conserved viral feature or a host process. The 2026 portfolio rationale explicitly emphasizes potent, safe, orally available antivirals; the 2023 review discusses resistance, toxicity, and clinical translation as continuing challenges.

Development synthesis: assembling a small formulary also requires establishing which medicines cover which viruses and populations, how treatment is selected before diagnosis, and where additional or alternative therapy is needed. A drug effective against one member of a family cannot automatically supply coverage for the rest. The number of regimens, their combined spectrum, and their practical boundaries remain design and validation questions.

current_state.text: Karim, Lo, and Einav's June 1, 2023 Journal of Clinical Investigation review documents effective antiviral treatments for several important infections, including HIV, hepatitis C, influenza, herpesvirus infections, and COVID-19. It also describes the generally narrow coverage of approved antivirals. These successes establish that particular viral infections can be treated effectively; they do not themselves establish the proposed small formulary for empiric treatment across major causes of severe acute RNA-virus disease.

The October 7, 2026 Nature Reviews Microbiology abstract by Thibaut and colleagues identifies continuing treatment gaps for many life-threatening viral infections, many caused by RNA viruses. It advocates a diversified portfolio with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families, and potentially multiple families. The supplied review verified this abstract, rather than the full article. It therefore supports the recent unmet need and portfolio rationale, but does not establish a complete clinical inventory or the categorical absence of every form of cross-family clinical efficacy.

The 2023 JCI review describes broad preclinical antiviral activity alongside limited or inconsistent translation into human benefit and important safety challenges. Its full text was available to the supplied evidence review. These examples support continued investigation of broad-spectrum approaches, while showing why laboratory protection cannot substitute for clinical outcomes. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate a formulary meeting this concept's proposed breadth, delivery, safety, and empiric-use requirements.

Evidence limitation: the research notes describe ESCRT-pathway compounds reportedly active against filoviruses and an enterovirus in cell assays, and attribute additional conclusions to 2026 Journal of Virology and 2025 Current Opinion in Virology reviews. The supplied evidence review had no retained source text verifying those particular results or attributions. They remain unverified research leads; if confirmed as described, the cell-assay findings would still be preclinical evidence. Missing documentation does not show that the reports are false.

The research also attributes a characterization of pan-viral agents as exceptionally uncommon and often discovered by chance to a 2025 Drug Discovery Today article. Its indexed landing-page URL has no captured document or retained text in the supplied source record, so that characterization and the article's identity were not verified by the review. Even a confirmed statement about the scarcity of such agents would not establish how often universal antiviral targets exist.

Assessment boundary: the supplied freshness record is empty, so the dated reviews cannot establish a comprehensive clinical-development landscape as of November 1, 2026. No supported completion timeline is available. The earlier numerical assertion about approximately 100 approved antivirals treating 10 of more than 200 human pathogenic viruses remains withdrawn because it was not re-verified; no replacement count is justified by the supplied evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: show clinical efficacy against severe acute disease using one practically deliverable regimen, or a prospectively bounded small formulary, across a specified set of major human RNA-virus families with unmet treatment needs. Include at least one family without an approved direct-acting antiviral. Before evaluation, define the family and virus list, relevant patient populations, meaning of effective existing treatment, maximum formulary size, and clinically meaningful outcome measures. These are proposed criteria for this concept, rather than established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Deliverable regimen or bounded formulary demonstrates efficacy across specified RNA-virus families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility requirement: demonstrate benefit in appropriately controlled clinical studies, with confirmation across independent studies or settings sufficient to establish reproducibility. Specify the viruses and populations actually tested within each family, and justify any extrapolation to untested relatives. Cell-culture panels and animal protection can support development but cannot complete the clinical demonstration. Finite testing establishes a documented breadth of efficacy, rather than literal coverage of every member of a family.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled clinical benefit reproduces across independent studies or settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed empiric-use demonstration: begin treatment before pathogen identification, subsequently confirm the causative virus, and show clinical benefit under that workflow. Replicate this across enough of the specified spectrum to establish the intended use. One successful unidentified-at-treatment infection would demonstrate an instance of empiric treatment; it would not establish effectiveness against arbitrary unknown viruses or future pathogens.
completion_criteria.label: Treatment before pathogen identification demonstrates benefit across the specified spectrum

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: demonstrate acceptable safety at effective exposures, feasible delivery in the intended care setting, and a prospectively defined low rate of treatment-emergent resistance during a normal course. Specify treatment timing, contraindications, relevant patient groups, coverage gaps, and rules for changing therapy when diagnostic results arrive. A putative universal RNA-and-DNA-virus agent would still need convincing clinical efficacy, safety, and reproducibility evidence; laboratory inhibition alone would not satisfy these requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Acceptable safety, feasible delivery, and prospectively defined low treatment-emergent resistance

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — VIR-01, A prospective sequence-to-phenotype theory of infectivity, transmission, and escape, could inform surveillance, resistance assessment, and prioritization of antiviral testing. VIR-08, A general experimental reading of viral genes that have no recognizable relatives, could reveal previously inaccessible drug targets or host dependencies. Both concern understanding and predicting viral biology; VIR-02 requires clinically effective medicines and a validated treatment workflow.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-03, Scalable elimination or permanent silencing of persistent viral genomes, addresses persistence and reservoirs beyond this acute-treatment concept. VIR-10, A single-dose, conditionally replicating interfering particle that keeps a chronic virus suppressed, concerns a particular therapeutic approach to sustained chronic control. VIR-11, An interruptible causal chain from a persistent virus to a major chronic disease, concerns causal understanding and intervention in chronic disease. These may share antiviral mechanisms or development tools with VIR-02, but acute suppression does not establish reservoir clearance, durable chronic control, or interruption of a chronic-disease pathway.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-04, Protective immunity that covers a viral family, including future variants and unseen relatives, shares the objective of breadth across related viruses but achieves protection through immunity. VIR-05, Durable immunity at the respiratory surface that stops transmission, targets sustained mucosal protection and transmission prevention. VIR-09, A mechanistic correlate that predicts human protection from a new virus, concerns predicting protective responses. VIR-02 instead requires evidence that administered medicines improve acute disease outcomes; that benefit would not by itself demonstrate durable immunity or stopped transmission.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-06, Bacteriophage therapy that can be prescribed as reliably as an antibacterial drug, shares the aim of dependable clinical prescribing, but uses viruses to treat bacterial infection. VIR-07, Viral particles that can be aimed at chosen human cells, given again, and carry large genes, concerns delivery technology that might support some therapeutic approaches. Neither reliable phage treatment nor improved viral delivery would by itself establish broad empiric treatment of acute human viral disease.

change_log.change: Retained VIR-02's identity and centered the concept on a clinically validated small formulary for empiric treatment of severe acute RNA-virus disease.
change_log.reason: Both the research and review support a portfolio approach without requiring a universal molecule or implying that the capability already exists.

change_log.change: Qualified the claim that viral diversity necessarily confines direct-acting drugs to narrow coverage and incorporated conserved polymerase catalytic structures as an exception.
change_log.reason: The supplied JCI review supports substantial viral diversity while identifying opportunities for broader direct-acting inhibition.

change_log.change: Integrated shared host dependencies, short-course safety, delivery, resistance, and preclinical-to-clinical translation into the missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why broad laboratory activity is insufficient for a usable empiric treatment.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical assertion that cross-family clinical coverage is absent with the narrower conclusion that the supplied evidence does not demonstrate the proposed formulary.
change_log.reason: The October 2026 abstract documents unmet need but does not provide a complete clinical inventory.

change_log.change: Preserved the ESCRT example and additional review attributions as explicitly unverified research leads, without treating them as established results.
change_log.reason: The supplied review lacked the supporting artifacts; that limitation warrants qualification rather than a conclusion that the reports are false.

change_log.change: Removed the asserted rarity of a universal antiviral site and the forecast that a portfolio would take longer than a single-target solution.
change_log.reason: Neither target frequency nor comparative development timing is established by the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Retained the antibiotic comparison as a bounded interpretive analogy and separated empiric use from efficacy against entirely novel viruses.
change_log.reason: Treatment before identification is the relevant comparison, while novelty and universal coverage require additional evidence.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to specify coverage, clinical outcomes, reproducibility, delivery, safety, resistance, and tested populations.
change_log.reason: The original proposal left major terms undefined and risked implying that one representative establishes family-wide coverage.

change_log.change: Kept the earlier antiviral and virus counts withdrawn and preserved the abstract-only, missing-document, and freshness limitations.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not justify restoring quantitative claims or presenting a comprehensive November 2026 landscape.

change_log.change: Added explicit relationships to every other supplied roster entry while retaining their distinct objectives.
change_log.reason: Shared mechanisms and development tools do not make acute antiviral treatment equivalent to immunity, reservoir elimination, chronic control, predictive theory, or delivery technology.

unresolved_issues: The major viral families, individual viruses, patient populations, and maximum number of regimens defining the proposed formulary remain unspecified.
Clinical efficacy endpoints, acceptable safety margins, treatment windows, and the proposed low resistance threshold require prospective definition.
The supplied evidence does not establish the complete clinical landscape as of November 1, 2026 or resolve whether any existing cross-family clinical applications meet part of the proposed scope.
The attributed Bayurova and Beran statements and the ESCRT-compound findings require supporting source text before they can be presented as verified evidence.
The Drug Discovery Today article's identity and attributed characterization remain unverified because no document text was captured.
Thibaut and colleagues' full review was not available in the supplied evidence assessment; its alleged characterization of a universal-drug slogan remains unverified.
The existence or feasibility of a safe universal RNA-and-DNA-virus target, and any completion timeline, remain unresolved.

The review's recommendation to omit unverified compound-specific material entirely was not adopted: the ESCRT example is retained only as an explicitly unverified research lead, preserving useful research detail without claiming an established achievement.
